questions.question: What are the three fundamental drivers of cost with AWS?

options.text: Compute, networking, and databases
Compute, storage, and outbound data transfer
EC2, S3, and RDS
On-Demand, Reserved, and Spot

explanation.correct: The three fundamental cost drivers are compute, storage, and outbound data transfer.
explanation.why: A is incorrect — networking is part of outbound data transfer. C lists services, not cost categories. D lists pricing models.

questions.question: Which AWS pricing model requires no upfront payment and no long-term commitment?

options.text: Reserved Instances
Spot Instances
On-Demand Instances
Dedicated Hosts

explanation.correct: On-Demand Instances charge by the hour with no upfront payment or long-term commitment.
explanation.why: Reserved Instances require a 1- or 3-year commitment. Spot Instances can be interrupted. Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive option.

questions.question: Up to how much can you save with Reserved Instances compared to On-Demand pricing?

options.text: Up to 30%
Up to 50%
Up to 72%
Up to 90%

explanation.correct: Reserved Instances can save up to 72% compared to equivalent On-Demand capacity.
explanation.why: Spot Instances can save up to 90%, but that's for a different pricing model. 72% is the maximum savings for Reserved Instances.

questions.question: Which EC2 pricing model is best for fault-tolerant batch processing jobs that can be interrupted?

options.text: On-Demand Instances
Reserved Instances
Dedicated Hosts
Spot Instances

explanation.correct: Spot Instances are ideal for fault-tolerant, flexible workloads that can be interrupted, offering the deepest discounts.
explanation.why: On-Demand is too expensive for this use case. Reserved requires long-term commitment. Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive option and designed for licensing compliance.

questions.question: What is the AWS Pricing Calculator used for?

options.text: Viewing historical spending in your AWS account
Estimating costs before deploying architecture
Automatically right-sizing EC2 instances
Auditing security vulnerabilities in your account

explanation.correct: The AWS Pricing Calculator helps you estimate costs for proposed AWS architecture before deploying.
explanation.why: A describes Cost Explorer. C is not a feature of the Pricing Calculator. D describes Trusted Advisor's security checks.

questions.question: Which S3 storage class uses physical tape drives and has retrieval times measured in hours?

options.text: S3 Standard-IA
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 One Zone-IA

explanation.correct: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest cost storage class and uses tape drives, with retrieval times of several hours.
explanation.why: Standard-IA has millisecond retrieval. Glacier Instant Retrieval offers millisecond access. One Zone-IA is fast but stored in a single AZ.

questions.question: AWS Trusted Advisor provides recommendations across how many categories?

options.text: Three
Four
Five
Six

explanation.correct: Trusted Advisor covers five categories: Cost Optimization, Performance, Security, Fault Tolerance, and Service Limits.
explanation.why: The Well-Architected Framework has six pillars, but Trusted Advisor specifically covers five check categories.

questions.question: Which AWS tool provides visual representations of your historical spending broken down by service and region?

options.text: AWS Pricing Calculator
AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Cost Explorer
AWS CloudWatch

explanation.correct: AWS Cost Explorer visualizes historical and current spending, with filtering by service, region, and linked accounts.
explanation.why: Pricing Calculator is for estimates before deploying. Trusted Advisor audits existing resources. CloudWatch monitors performance metrics, not billing.

questions.question: Cost Optimization is one pillar of the AWS Well-Architected Framework. How many total pillars are there?

options.text: Four
Five
Six
Seven

explanation.correct: The AWS Well-Architected Framework has six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability.
explanation.why: Sustainability was added as the sixth pillar a few years ago, making the total count six.

questions.question: Which pricing model requires you to pay for an entire physical server dedicated solely to your account?

options.text: Dedicated Instance
Dedicated Host
Reserved Instance
On-Demand Instance

explanation.correct: A Dedicated Host gives you an entire physical server reserved for your use, which is necessary for certain software licenses tied to hardware fingerprints.
explanation.why: A Dedicated Instance runs on dedicated hardware but AWS can move it between servers. Reserved and On-Demand run on shared infrastructure.

questions.question: A company has production EC2 instances running 24/7 for the past year and expects the same usage for the next two years. What pricing strategy offers the best cost savings?

options.text: On-Demand Instances for maximum flexibility
Spot Instances for maximum discounts
3-year Reserved Instances for the highest commitment discount
Dedicated Hosts to ensure consistent performance

explanation.correct: 3-year Reserved Instances offer the maximum discount (up to 72%) for steady, predictable workloads. Since the company knows they'll run these instances for 2+ more years, a 3-year commitment maximizes savings.
explanation.why: On-Demand is the most expensive for steady-state usage. Spot is inappropriate for always-on production workloads due to interruption risk. Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive option.

questions.question: Which S3 lifecycle policy configuration best optimizes cost for web application access logs that are actively analyzed for 30 days, then rarely accessed until annual audits, and must be retained for 7 years?

options.text: Keep all logs in S3 Standard for 7 years
Move to Standard-IA after 30 days, then to Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year
Delete all logs after 30 days to save costs
Move to Glacier Deep Archive immediately on creation

explanation.correct: This tiering strategy matches storage class to access pattern: Standard for active analysis (0-30 days), Standard-IA for the occasional audit access phase (30 days - 1 year), then Deep Archive for long-term retention at minimal cost.
explanation.why: A wastes money keeping rarely accessed data in expensive Standard storage. C violates retention requirements. D makes recently active logs very expensive and slow to retrieve.

questions.question: A developer ran EC2 instances in a region they don't normally use for a test last month, resulting in an unexpectedly high bill. Which tool would best help identify this going forward?

options.text: AWS Pricing Calculator
AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Cost Explorer with region filter
AWS CloudFormation

explanation.correct: AWS Cost Explorer with region filtering would clearly show the unexpected spend in the unfamiliar region, making it easy to identify and act on.
explanation.why: Pricing Calculator is for future estimates. Trusted Advisor flags underutilized resources but doesn't visualize historical spend by region as effectively. CloudFormation is infrastructure-as-code, not a cost tool.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid way to reduce costs for an Amazon RDS database instance?

options.text: Stop the instance during off-hours
Purchase a Reserved Instance for it
Convert it to a Spot Instance
Right-size to a smaller instance type

explanation.correct: Spot Instances are only available for EC2, not for RDS. RDS does not support the Spot pricing model.
explanation.why: Stopping RDS, purchasing Reserved Instances, and right-sizing are all valid RDS cost reduction strategies. Only Spot is unavailable for RDS.

questions.question: A startup is building a new application and doesn't yet know what their compute requirements will be in production. What is the recommended initial approach?

options.text: Purchase 3-year Reserved Instances immediately to lock in the best price
Use On-Demand Instances, monitor with CloudWatch, then move to Reserved once usage is understood
Use the largest instance type available to ensure the app has enough resources
Use Dedicated Hosts to ensure maximum performance

explanation.correct: Starting with On-Demand gives flexibility while you learn usage patterns. Once you've established a stable baseline, you can convert to Reserved Instances for significant savings.
explanation.why: Committing to 3-year Reserved Instances before knowing requirements can lead to over-provisioning or misaligned instance types. Over-sizing wastes money. Dedicated Hosts are expensive and designed for licensing needs, not general best practice.

questions.question: What does 'right-sizing' mean in the context of AWS Cost Optimization?

options.text: Ensuring all instances are the same size for consistency
Matching instance size to actual workload requirements based on utilization data
Purchasing the largest possible instance to avoid performance issues
Using only t2.micro instances to stay within the free tier

explanation.correct: Right-sizing means selecting the instance size that matches your actual workload needs, using CloudWatch metrics to inform decisions rather than guessing or over-provisioning.
explanation.why: Consistency is not the goal — matching each workload's needs is. Over-provisioning wastes money. Using only t2.micro ignores actual requirements.

questions.question: Why does AWS charge for public IPv4 addresses (approximately $3.60/month each)?

options.text: IPv4 addresses are scarce and expensive to maintain
To encourage customer migration to IPv6 while covering real costs
IPv4 addresses require more bandwidth than IPv6
To generate additional revenue during peak demand periods

explanation.correct: AWS introduced IPv4 pricing both to reflect the real cost of increasingly scarce IPv4 addresses and to guide customer behavior toward IPv6 adoption.
explanation.why: While scarcity is part of it, the primary stated goal is behavior shaping — encouraging IPv6 migration. IPv4 vs IPv6 has no bandwidth difference. The charge applies consistently, not just during peak periods.

questions.question: An S3 Lifecycle Policy is configured to move objects to Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days of no access. A user urgently needs a file that was moved to Glacier 6 months ago. What is the tradeoff?

options.text: No tradeoff — Glacier Flexible Retrieval has instant access
The file will be deleted after 90 days in Glacier
Retrieval will take minutes to hours and incur retrieval fees
The file cannot be retrieved once moved to Glacier

explanation.correct: Glacier Flexible Retrieval offers minutes to hours retrieval time (depending on the retrieval tier chosen) and charges retrieval fees in addition to storage costs.
explanation.why: Glacier Instant Retrieval has near-instant access, but Flexible Retrieval does not. Files in Glacier are not automatically deleted. Glacier is an archive, not a deletion — data remains retrievable.

questions.question: Which AWS service automatically detects underutilized EC2 instances and recommends cost-saving actions in your existing account?

options.text: AWS Pricing Calculator
AWS Trusted Advisor
Amazon CloudFormation
Amazon CloudFront

explanation.correct: AWS Trusted Advisor continuously monitors your account and flags underutilized EC2 instances, idle load balancers, unattached EBS volumes, and other waste.
explanation.why: Pricing Calculator is for pre-deployment estimates. CloudFormation is infrastructure-as-code. CloudFront is a CDN service.

questions.question: A company uses EC2 Auto Scaling for their web tier. During a 6-month analysis, they find that 70% of their capacity runs 24/7, while the remaining 30% only runs during business hours. What is the optimal pricing strategy?

options.text: On-Demand for all instances
Reserved Instances for the 70% baseline, On-Demand or Spot for the 30% variable portion
Spot Instances for all 100% of capacity
Reserved Instances for 100% of peak capacity

explanation.correct: This mixed strategy is a well-architected best practice: use Reserved Instances for the predictable, always-on baseline (maximum savings), and On-Demand or Spot for variable, scaling capacity.
explanation.why: All On-Demand wastes the savings opportunity on the stable 70%. All Spot is inappropriate for production web servers due to interruption risk. Reserving 100% of peak capacity wastes money when the extra 30% isn't running.

questions.question: A company running a data analytics workload finds that their Redshift cluster is only queried 8 hours per day on weekdays. What is the most cost-effective approach?

options.text: Purchase Redshift Reserved Instances for the maximum discount
Pause the Redshift cluster when not actively querying and resume on demand
Move all data to S3 Standard and run ad-hoc queries
Migrate to a larger Redshift cluster for better query performance

explanation.correct: Pausing Redshift stops compute charges while preserving all data. For 8 hours/day on weekdays (~40 hours/week out of 168), the cluster is idle 76% of the time — pausing during that idle time provides massive savings.
explanation.why: Reserved Instances still charge whether the cluster is used or not. Moving to S3 alone would lose the Redshift query engine. Larger clusters increase cost without addressing the idle time problem.

questions.question: How does the AWS Cost Optimization pillar's principle of 'matching capacity with demand' differ from traditional on-premises capacity planning?

options.text: There is no difference — both require provisioning for peak demand
AWS allows dynamic scaling to actual demand, eliminating over-provisioning for peak loads
AWS requires you to provision capacity one year in advance
On-premises is always cheaper because you own the hardware

explanation.correct: AWS enables dynamic capacity matching through Auto Scaling, serverless services, and on-demand provisioning — eliminating the traditional requirement to provision for worst-case peak demand and pay for idle capacity year-round.
explanation.why: Traditional on-premises absolutely requires provisioning for peak. AWS doesn't require advance planning in the same way — you scale as needed. On-premises has higher total cost of ownership when accounting for CapEx, maintenance, and idle capacity.

questions.question: A financial services company must retain transaction records for 10 years for regulatory compliance. The records are accessed frequently in the first 30 days (auditing), occasionally between 30 days and 2 years (investigations), and essentially never after 2 years unless a major audit occurs. What S3 configuration minimizes cost while meeting requirements?

options.text: S3 Standard for all 10 years
S3 Standard for 30 days → Standard-IA for 30 days to 2 years → Glacier Deep Archive for 2 to 10 years
S3 Glacier Deep Archive from day one for maximum savings
Delete records after 2 years since they're rarely accessed

explanation.correct: This tiered approach matches each storage class to the actual access pattern: Standard for active use, Standard-IA for occasional access (pays retrieval fee only when needed), and Deep Archive for long-term retention at minimal cost.
explanation.why: All Standard wastes significant money on 8+ years of cold data. Glacier from day one means slow, expensive retrieval during the first 30 days of active use. Deleting at 2 years violates the 10-year compliance requirement.

questions.question: A startup uses the AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate $2,500/month for their initial architecture. Six months after launch, AWS Cost Explorer shows actual monthly spend of $4,100. What are the most likely causes of this gap?

options.text: AWS increased prices after the estimate was created
The Pricing Calculator is not reliable and should not be used
Actual data transfer volumes exceeded estimates, plus additional services were added after launch
The startup is being charged for other companies' usage

explanation.correct: The most common causes of estimate-vs-reality gaps are underestimated data transfer volumes (which are hard to predict before launch) and additional services added organically as the application grows.
explanation.why: AWS has cut prices over 70 times — they don't increase prices. The Pricing Calculator is reliable for what was estimated, but can't predict what wasn't modeled. AWS billing is per-account and isolated.

questions.question: Which combination of tools provides the most comprehensive cost management strategy across the full application lifecycle?

options.text: AWS Pricing Calculator only — plan everything upfront
AWS Cost Explorer only — monitor spending after deployment
Pricing Calculator (pre-deployment) + Trusted Advisor (ongoing audit) + Cost Explorer (spend analysis)
Manual spreadsheets for tracking all AWS expenses

explanation.correct: A comprehensive cost strategy requires all three: Pricing Calculator for pre-deployment planning, Trusted Advisor for proactive waste detection, and Cost Explorer for historical analysis and trend monitoring.
explanation.why: Any single tool alone creates blind spots. Manual spreadsheets can't match the real-time granularity of native AWS tools.

questions.question: AWS charges for outbound data transfer but generally not for inbound. Which architectural pattern would help a company minimize outbound data transfer costs?

options.text: Keep all compute and storage in different regions to maximize redundancy
Process data closer to where it's stored using services in the same region or AZ
Send all data through an on-premises data center before delivering to end users
Use dedicated network lines for all data transfers

explanation.correct: Data transfer between services within the same region (and especially same AZ) is free or very cheap. Processing data where it lives minimizes cross-region and internet-bound data transfer charges.
explanation.why: Cross-region deployments actually increase data transfer costs significantly. Routing through on-premises adds latency and complexity. Dedicated lines (Direct Connect) are for reducing internet data transfer costs but add their own charges.

questions.question: A company is evaluating whether to use Amazon RDS Aurora or a self-managed MySQL database on EC2. From a cost optimization perspective, what is a key consideration?

options.text: Aurora is always more expensive and should be avoided
EC2-based MySQL requires you to manage, patch, and scale the database yourself, which has hidden operational costs
Self-managed databases on EC2 qualify for Reserved Instance discounts but Aurora does not
Aurora and EC2 MySQL have identical total cost of ownership

explanation.correct: While Aurora may have a higher compute price, self-managed databases require significant operational overhead — managing backups, patches, failover, and scaling — which has real labor costs that are often overlooked in pure infrastructure comparisons.
explanation.why: Aurora is not universally more expensive — managed services can be cheaper when operational costs are factored in. Both can use Reserved Instances. TCO is never identical when one requires manual management.

questions.question: An engineering team notices their AWS bill has been increasing 15% month-over-month for three months. They have not launched any new services. What should be their first investigative step?

options.text: Immediately switch all instances to Spot to reduce costs
Use Cost Explorer to identify which service and region is driving the increase, then use Trusted Advisor for optimization recommendations
Contact AWS support to dispute the charges
Purchase Reserved Instances for all services immediately

explanation.correct: The correct approach is to first diagnose (Cost Explorer for what and where) before prescribing a solution. Once the source of growth is identified, Trusted Advisor can surface specific optimization actions.
explanation.why: Switching to Spot without understanding the cause is reactive and risky. Disputing charges is appropriate only for billing errors, not usage growth. Buying Reserved Instances before understanding the cost driver could lock in the wrong configuration.

questions.question: How does Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering reduce costs compared to S3 Standard?

options.text: It compresses all objects automatically to reduce storage footprint
It monitors access patterns and automatically moves objects to lower-cost tiers when they haven't been accessed recently
It replicates data across fewer availability zones to reduce storage costs
It charges lower retrieval fees than S3 Standard

explanation.correct: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between frequent and infrequent access tiers based on actual access patterns, eliminating the need to manually manage lifecycle policies when access patterns are unknown or variable.
explanation.why: S3 does not automatically compress objects. Intelligent-Tiering still uses multiple AZs for durability. S3 Standard has no retrieval fees — the charge comparison is on storage price, not retrieval.

questions.question: A Well-Architected Review flags that a company is running 15 EC2 instances with average CPU utilization below 5% over the past 30 days. What is the most appropriate response according to Cost Optimization best practices?

options.text: This is acceptable — underutilized instances provide a safety buffer for traffic spikes
Analyze actual usage patterns, right-size or consolidate instances, and implement Auto Scaling to handle spikes dynamically
Immediately terminate all 15 instances to save costs
Move all 15 instances to Dedicated Hosts for better resource utilization

explanation.correct: The correct response is to analyze first, then act: understand what these instances do, right-size to appropriate smaller types, potentially consolidate workloads, and use Auto Scaling to handle genuine spikes rather than idle over-provisioning.
explanation.why: Accepting 5% utilization as normal is wasteful — it suggests significant over-provisioning. Immediate termination without analysis could disrupt running services. Dedicated Hosts are more expensive, not less.

questions.question: What is a Compute Savings Plan and which services does it apply to?

options.text: A discount for buying EC2 hardware outright; applies to EC2 only
A commitment-based discount that applies to EC2, AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda
A government program for startups to get free AWS credits
An automatic cost reduction applied when you use multiple AWS services together

explanation.correct: Compute Savings Plans are a flexible commitment-based model where you commit to a consistent amount of compute usage (in $/hour), and the discount applies automatically across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda.
explanation.why: Savings Plans are not hardware purchases. They are not government programs. Discounts from Savings Plans are commitment-based, not automatic multi-service discounts.
